label: Chapter 6: Leopold's Capital, the Belle Époque and the Congo, 1831 to 1914

units.text: The new Belgium turned out to be a remarkable success story, and Brussels was its showcase.
Belgium was the first country on the European continent to undergo an industrial revolution, following the example of Britain.
Coal and iron in the south, textiles in Flanders, and a good banking system created real wealth.
In 1835, the first railway on the continent opened between Brussels and the nearby city of Mechelen, and within a few years, the country had a dense network of tracks, with Brussels at the center.
The population grew fast, and the capital swelled with civil servants, bankers, merchants, and workers.
The city also became a haven for ideas, and for exiles.
In 1834, liberal Brussels founded a new university, the Free University of Brussels, dedicated to free inquiry, independent of both state and church.
Because the new Belgian constitution was so liberal, the city attracted writers, thinkers, and political refugees from across Europe.
The French poet Charles Baudelaire stayed there, and so did the novelist Victor Hugo, who lived for a time on the Grand Place.
In 1873, in a Brussels hotel room, the poet Paul Verlaine shot and wounded his young lover, the poet Arthur Rimbaud, and then went to jail in Belgium.
One exile, above all, left a mark.
In 1845, the young German philosopher Karl Marx, expelled from France, came to Brussels with his wife and family, and he stayed until 1848.
With his friend Friedrich Engels, he wrote a pamphlet in Brussels, in the winter of 1847 and 1848, called the Manifesto of the Communist Party.
It was published in London in February of 1848, and Marx was expelled from Belgium a few weeks later.
The pamphlet he wrote there went on to shape the history of the twentieth century.
Meanwhile, the city itself was in trouble.
The Senne river, which had made Brussels possible, had become a disaster.
It ran through the middle of the city, an open sewer, choked with refuse, and it flooded regularly.
It carried cholera. The stench in summer was notorious.
In the 1860s, the city's reforming mayor, Jules Anspach, decided to bury it.
Between 1867 and 1871, the river was covered with a long brick vault, and above it, the city built a grand new avenue lined with elegant buildings, modeled on the Paris boulevards of Baron Haussmann.
That avenue is called the Boulevard Anspach, after the mayor who built it.
The river is still there today, flowing in a tunnel beneath the city.
In the nineteenth century, they built a Stock Exchange, the Bourse, in the heart of the new district, and the whole center was transformed.
It was an enormous achievement, and also a loss: hundreds of old houses and streets in the working-class neighborhoods were torn down, and whole communities were uprooted.
There was another giant project.
In 1866, work began on a vast new Palace of Justice, designed by the architect Joseph Poelaert, on a hill above the Marolles.

When it was finished in 1883, it was often described as the largest building constructed anywhere in the nineteenth century, a colossal mass of columns, domes, and staircases that dwarfs the city around it.
To build it, authorities flattened part of the old working-class Marolles district.
Locals have grumbled about it ever since.
In 1865, Leopold the First died, and his son took the throne as Leopold the Second.
Leopold the Second reigned for forty-four years, and he was ambitious in a way that his father was not.
He felt that his country was too small, and he dreamed of an empire.
The great European powers were carving up Africa, and Leopold wanted a piece of it.
At a conference in Berlin in 1884 and 1885, the great powers recognized Leopold as the ruler of a vast territory in central Africa, about eighty times the size of Belgium.
This territory was not a Belgian colony.
It was the king's personal property, called the Congo Free State.
And what followed was one of the worst atrocities of the colonial era.
Leopold's agents forced villagers to collect rubber and ivory, under a system of terror: hostages were taken, villages burned, and people who failed to meet quotas were beaten, mutilated, or killed.
Historians estimate that millions of Congolese died from violence, starvation, and disease during these years, although the exact numbers are debated.
Reports by missionaries, journalists, and the British diplomat Roger Casement, and a campaign led by the journalist Edmund Morel, eventually produced an international outcry.
In 1908, under heavy pressure, the Belgian state took over the colony from the king, and it became the Belgian Congo, which Belgium ruled until 1960.
The money that Leopold drew from the Congo went partly into Brussels.
He used it to build, and to impress.
He built the great Cinquantenaire park and its triumphal arch, to commemorate fifty years of Belgian independence.
He built wide avenues, such as Avenue Louise, and monuments, and royal greenhouses at Laeken, and a huge museum of Central Africa in the suburb of Tervuren.
For the Brussels world's fair of 1897, he organized a colonial exhibition in which Congolese people were put on display in a replica village.
The grand showpiece of Belgium's capital had been paid for, in part, by a terrible human cost, and that is a story that Brussels has been grappling with ever since.
In the same decades, a very different kind of beauty emerged in Brussels.
In the 1890s, a group of young architects, led by Victor Horta, created a new style that rejected the heavy historical imitations of the time.
They used iron, glass, and sweeping curves inspired by plants and flowers, in what came to be known as Art Nouveau, or the new art.

In 1893 and 1894, Horta built a townhouse for a professor named Emile Tassel, in which iron columns shaped like stems and stairs twining like vines flowed through the whole house, with light pouring in from above.
It is widely regarded as the first Art Nouveau building.
Other architects, including Paul Hankar and Henry van de Velde, followed.
The style spread to Paris, Vienna, and Barcelona, but it started in Brussels.
Several of Horta's townhouses are now a UNESCO World Heritage site.
By 1900, Brussels was a prosperous, confident metropolis of more than half a million people in its wider urban area, a city of cafés, department stores, glass-roofed shopping arcades, and boulevards.
It was also a French-speaking city.

At the time of independence, a large share of ordinary Brusselers spoke a Dutch dialect, but French was the language of government, business, education, and prestige, and over the nineteenth century, it steadily took over.
Today the city is officially bilingual, and the question of language, which was just beginning to stir in the late nineteenth century, will return again and again in the story of modern Belgium.
But the fates of small countries rest on the decisions of large ones.
The guarantee of Belgian neutrality, signed in 1839, was now seventy-five years old.
And in the summer of 1914, a crisis in the Balkans pushed Europe toward war.
Germany's plan to defeat France called for an army to march through neutral Belgium.
If you want to see this chapter in stone, walk the Boulevard Anspach and look at the grand facades of the Bourse.
Visit the Palace of Justice, whose terrace has a famous view over the whole city.
And if you have time for one museum, make it the Horta Museum in Saint-Gilles, which is the house where the architect lived and worked.
